notes: PCN moved from MD slot 13 to ruling slot 0 (it is Sanchez Hernandez's governing party and firmly pro-US). PDC kept in MD slot 2. Slot 13 coalition partner filled with the CONAPLAN planning technocracy that runs the regime's reform agenda. Islamic slots and slots 6, 17, 19, 20, 23 are catchy factions rooted in real milieus.

0.name: Partido de Conciliación Nacional
0.text:
The National Conciliation Party was founded in 1961 by the officers who seized power that year, and it has governed El Salvador ever since as the political arm of the armed forces. President Fidel Sánchez Hernández, elected in 1967, leads the country out of the July 1969 war with Honduras riding a wave of patriotic support ahead of the March 1970 elections.

The PCN offers controlled reform within an anti-communist order: Alliance for Progress development, Central American Common Market industry and close ties to Washington, while leaving coffee estates untouched. Its strength lies in the officer corps, the state payroll, rural patronage and the ORDEN network, which deliver votes in the countryside year after year.

1.name: Partido Popular Salvadoreño
1.text:
The Salvadoran Popular Party was founded in the mid-1960s by conservatives who found the official PCN too willing to flirt with reform. It sits in the Legislative Assembly as a small right-wing opposition and prepares to contest the March 1970 legislative and municipal elections.

The PPS defends private property, the coffee economy and an uncompromising anti-communism, and it warns that any agrarian reform would open the door to Cuban-style revolution. It looks to the United States as the guarantor of order. Its voters are urban property owners, merchants and landed families, and its leverage comes from business money and from the fear that the regime might drift too far to the centre.

2.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
2.text:
The Christian Democratic Party was founded in 1960 and has become the strongest opposition force in El Salvador. Its leading figure, José Napoleón Duarte, has been mayor of San Salvador since 1964 and turned the capital into a showcase of competent, honest administration that the military regime cannot ignore.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching, the PDC calls for agrarian reform, fair elections, labour rights and community development, positioning itself as the democratic alternative to both military rule and communist revolution. It is friendly to the United States and its reformist rhetoric. The party draws on the urban middle class, Catholic lay movements and growing numbers of workers, and its leverage lies in winning cities and Assembly seats.

3.name: Movimiento Nacional Revolucionario
3.text:
The National Revolutionary Movement was founded in 1965 by university professionals and intellectuals seeking a democratic socialist option for El Salvador. It is a small legal party led by the lawyer Guillermo Manuel Ungo, son of a founder of the Christian Democrats, and it has a modest presence in the Assembly.

The MNR advocates agrarian reform, progressive taxation, free trade unions and an end to military tutelage, modelling itself on European social democracy. It is critical of US backing for the regime but rejects the Soviet road. Its base is narrow, made up of lecturers, lawyers, teachers and students, and its leverage lies in ideas and in alliances with the larger PDC.

4.name: Partido Comunista de El Salvador
4.text:
The Communist Party of El Salvador was founded in 1930 and led the 1932 uprising that ended in the Matanza. Banned ever since, it operates underground, with Schafik Jorge Hándal among its leading cadres and Salvador Cayetano Carpio as its general secretary. The party leadership is quarrelling over whether to pursue elections or armed struggle.

Loyal to Moscow, the PCS pursues a broad democratic front, working through legal fronts such as the UDN and through trade unions, teachers and students. It condemns US imperialism and the coffee oligarchy. Its influence lies in organised labour, the ANDES teachers' movement and the National University, not in mass membership.

5.name: Asociación General de Estudiantes Universitarios Salvadoreños
5.english: General Association of Salvadoran University Students
5.native_full: Asociación General de Estudiantes Universitarios Salvadoreños
5.text:
The General Association of Salvadoran University Students has represented students at the National University since 1927 and has helped topple dictators before. In 1970 it is a hotbed of radical politics, where Marxist study circles, Guevarist admirers of the Cuban Revolution and Christian radicals argue over the road to power.

AGEUS denounces the military regime, the coffee oligarchy and US influence, and many of its activists now regard elections as a trap and armed struggle as inevitable. Its leverage lies in street mobilisation, the autonomous university campus and its role as a training ground for the cadres of a coming generation of guerrilla organisations.

6.name: Las Catorce Familias
6.text:
The Fourteen Families is the popular name for the handful of interlinked clans who own the best coffee land, the processing plants and the banks of El Salvador. Since 1932 they have ceded political office to the army in exchange for protection of their estates, and they watch the reform talk of 1970 with deep suspicion.

This hardline core of the oligarchy rejects every form of agrarian reform and resents Alliance for Progress pressure from Washington as meddling by naïve gringos. It wants a firm hand against unions and priests alike. Its leverage is immense: export earnings, credit, newspapers and personal ties to senior officers who can be persuaded to remove any president who goes too far.

7.name: Agencia Nacional de Seguridad Salvadoreña
7.text:
The Salvadoran National Security Agency was created in the mid-1960s as an intelligence service attached to the presidency, built up by General José Alberto Medrano with American advice. It collects files on union leaders, priests, students and opposition politicians and coordinates the security forces and the rural informant networks.

ANSESAL sees subversion everywhere and treats politics as a counter-insurgency problem to be managed through surveillance, lists and pressure. Its power is invisible but real: it controls information, decides who is a threat and can make careers or end them, and it gives whoever controls it a decisive say inside the regime.

8.name: Círculo de Baalbek
8.text:
The Baalbek Circle is a small gathering of Lebanese Shia merchants and their sons in San Salvador and Santa Ana, part of the wider Levantine trading community. They meet in private homes for religious holidays and follow news from Lebanon, where Imam Musa al-Sadr has just founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council.

The circle admires al-Sadr's message of dignity, education and social justice for the poor, and favours integration and good relations with the Salvadoran state. It is far from politics, but its commercial networks, remittances and links to the Lebanese diaspora across Latin America give it quiet economic weight.

9.name: Los Discípulos de Nayaf
9.text:
The Disciples of Najaf are a handful of young Shia of Lebanese origin who have studied or travelled in Iraq and returned with cassette recordings and pamphlets from the seminaries of Najaf. There, the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has just lectured on the idea of government by the Islamic jurist.

The group regards both the American and Soviet blocs as oppressors and dreams of a revolutionary Islamic order. In El Salvador it has no realistic political prospects and keeps to itself, but its fervour unsettles the community elders and its contacts abroad could make it useful to outside patrons.

10.name: La Cofradía del Hajj
10.text:
The Hajj Brotherhood is a loose association of Sunni Muslim Palestinian and Syrian families in El Salvador who have made the pilgrimage to Mecca and maintain contacts with the Muslim World League in Saudi Arabia. They organise prayers, Quran lessons for children and small charitable collections.

The brotherhood preaches obedience to legitimate authority, moral conservatism and staying out of politics, and it shares the government's anti-communism. Its leverage lies in respectable wealth, connections to Gulf patrons and the community's commercial standing, which give it access to ministers when its members need a favour.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
The Students of the Caliphate are a tiny group of young men of Palestinian origin who encountered the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir while studying in Amman and Beirut. Inspired by the writings of Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, they meet secretly to discuss the restoration of a single Islamic state.

They reject nationalism, democracy and both superpowers as man-made idols and call on Muslims everywhere to work for the caliphate. In El Salvador they are a curiosity with no social base, but they are disciplined, secretive and convinced that history is on their side.

12.name: Los Lectores de Qutb
12.text:
The Readers of Qutb are a small study circle of educated Muslims of Arab descent in San Salvador who read the works of Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, executed in Egypt in 1966. They are mostly professionals and university students who keep in touch with Muslim Brotherhood sympathisers in the Middle East.

The circle advocates personal piety, charitable work and an Islamic social order built from below through education. It is wary of both American capitalism and Soviet atheism. Its influence in El Salvador is minimal, limited to community schools and welfare among the Muslim minority.

13.name: Consejo Nacional de Planificación y Coordinación Económica
13.english: National Council for Economic Planning and Coordination
13.native_full: Consejo Nacional de Planificación y Coordinación Económica
13.text:
The National Council for Economic Planning and Coordination was set up in 1962 by the military government to steer development and manage Alliance for Progress funds. Staffed by economists, engineers and administrators, it drafts the five-year plans of the Sánchez Hernández administration and its cautious agrarian and educational reforms.

The planners believe El Salvador's problems are technical: overpopulation, land shortage and dependence on coffee can be solved through industrialisation, infrastructure and expertise rather than ideology. They serve the regime loyally but look beyond the blocs for models. Their leverage lies in budgets, foreign aid and the president's need for a modernising agenda after the war with Honduras.

14.name: Asociación Cafetalera de El Salvador
14.english: Coffee Growers Association of El Salvador
14.text:
The Coffee Growers Association of El Salvador was founded in 1930 and speaks for the planters whose harvest earns most of the country's foreign exchange. It brings together great estate owners and medium growers in the western highlands, and it negotiates prices, credit and export policy with every government.

The association defends the existing land structure, low rural wages and minimal state interference in the coffee economy, while demanding infrastructure and favourable exchange rates. Its conservatism is rooted in the countryside and the Church rather than in foreign alignment. Its leverage is economic: no government can survive a hostile coffee sector.

15.name: Asociación Nacional de la Empresa Privada
15.native_full: Asociación Nacional de la Empresa Privada
15.text:
The National Association of Private Enterprise was founded in 1966 as the umbrella organisation of Salvadoran business, uniting the chambers of commerce, industry, agriculture, banking and construction. It speaks for the great family groups that dominate the economy and has quickly become the private sector's voice to the state.

ANEP champions free enterprise, low taxes and the Central American Common Market, now shaken by the war with Honduras, and it opposes land reform and independent unions. Its leverage comes from investment decisions, bank credit and the close personal ties between its leaders and the senior officers who run the government.

16.name: Cámara de Comercio e Industria de El Salvador
16.english: Chamber of Commerce and Industry of El Salvador
16.native_full: Cámara de Comercio e Industria de El Salvador
16.text:
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of El Salvador, founded in 1915, represents importers, retailers and the new manufacturers who have prospered under the Central American Common Market. In 1970 its members are alarmed by the closure of the Honduran border and the collapse of regional trade after the 1969 war.

The chamber stands for free trade, open markets, sound money and limited government, and it opposes price controls and bureaucratic red tape. It favours close commercial ties with the United States. Its base is the urban merchant and industrial class of San Salvador, and its leverage lies in trade, employment and lobbying.

17.name: Defensores del Lempa
17.text:
The Defenders of the Lempa are a loose alliance of agronomists, biology teachers, parish priests and peasant families concerned about the fate of El Salvador's great river. Plans for a large hydroelectric dam at Cerrón Grande threaten to flood farmland and villages, while deforestation and erosion are stripping the country's hillsides.

They call for reforestation, soil protection, compensation for displaced communities and limits on pesticides in the cotton zones of the coast. They do not engage in bloc politics. Their leverage is small, resting on parish networks, the National University and local resistance in the affected river valleys.

18.name: Unión Democrática Nacionalista
18.text:
The Nationalist Democratic Union is a legal left-wing party registered in the late 1960s, widely seen as the electoral face of the banned Communist Party. It brings together trade unionists, teachers, students and progressive professionals, and it is preparing to contest the March 1970 elections.

The UDN calls for agrarian reform, nationalisation of key services, labour rights and an independent foreign policy free from US tutelage. It presents itself as a broad national-democratic front rather than a communist party. Its leverage lies in union halls, the teachers' movement and the hope of building a wider opposition coalition with the PDC and MNR.

19.name: Fracción Marcial
19.text:
Marcial's Faction gathers the Communist Party members who follow general secretary Salvador Cayetano Carpio, known by the nom de guerre Marcial, in rejecting the party's electoral line. A former baker and union leader, Carpio is increasingly at odds with the pro-Moscow majority and is preparing to break away.

The faction argues that the Salvadoran oligarchy can only be defeated through a prolonged people's war of workers and peasants, drawing on Vietnamese, Chinese and Cuban experience rather than Soviet caution. Its leverage lies in a small core of hardened cadres, union veterans and radical students ready to go underground.

20.name: Los Medranistas
20.text:
The Medranistas are the followers of General José Alberto Medrano, the National Guard commander celebrated as a hero of the 1969 war with Honduras and the founder of ORDEN and ANSESAL. His growing popularity and ambition put him increasingly at odds with President Sánchez Hernández.

The faction blends fierce nationalism, anti-communism and populist appeals to peasants and veterans, demanding a strong hand at home and firmness toward Honduras. It is pro-American in outlook but resents the officer clique around the president. Its leverage lies in Medrano's personal prestige, rural militia loyalties and contacts in the security services.

21.name: Organización Democrática Nacionalista
21.text:
The Nationalist Democratic Organization is a rural paramilitary network created in the mid-1960s by General José Alberto Medrano under the National Guard. It enrols tens of thousands of peasants, former soldiers and village notables as informants and auxiliaries, rewarding them with jobs, land titles and protection.

ORDEN exists to root out communism in the countryside through surveillance, intimidation and violence against organisers, catechists and union activists. It also mobilises votes for the PCN. Its leverage lies in its sheer reach into every canton and its fusion with the security forces, making it the regime's eyes and fist in rural El Salvador.

22.name: Fuerza Armada de El Salvador
22.text:
The Armed Forces of El Salvador have been the arbiters of national politics since 1931, choosing presidents and removing them when necessary. Fresh from the 1969 war with Honduras, in which the army advanced deep into Honduran territory before an OAS ceasefire, the institution enjoys unusual prestige in 1970.

The officer corps is anti-communist, trained and equipped with US assistance, and united by the graduating classes of the Military School. It guards the existing order while allowing limited reform. Its leverage is decisive: it controls the PCN, the security forces and the presidency, and no civilian force can govern without its consent.

23.name: Señorío de Cuscatlán
23.text:
The Lordship of Cuscatlán is the memory of the pre-Hispanic Pipil realm kept alive in the Nahua-speaking communities of Izalco, Nahuizalco and Panchimalco. Its institutions survive in the Alcaldía del Común of Izalco and the religious cofradías, whose hereditary elders still command authority despite the trauma of 1932.

The traditionalists seek recognition of indigenous authority, communal lands and customs, and protection of Nahuat language and culture. They distrust both the oligarchy and the revolutionaries. Their influence is local and ceremonial, but they hold the loyalty of indigenous villages in the western departments.
